medium.conteudo_html:
Building enterprise applications on Salesforce has always required two things simultaneously: deep platform knowledge and strong development skills.

You cannot just be a good JavaScript developer and drop into Lightning Web Component work. You need to understand how the wire service works, which properties are reactive and which are not, how to handle errors from @wire adapters, and how to build components that behave correctly when data is loading, loaded, and errored. You also need to know the Salesforce-specific restrictions that do not exist anywhere else in web development.

The same depth requirement applies to Apex. Writing Apex is not just writing Java. It is writing Java inside a constrained execution environment where CPU milliseconds are capped per transaction, SOQL queries are capped per execution context, DML operations are limited, and every trigger must be written to handle bulk operations without degrading — because Salesforce will batch data in ways your test coverage did not anticipate.

This depth requirement is what makes Salesforce developers valuable and what makes them hard to find, train, and retain. And it is what general-purpose AI coding assistants have struggled with — producing syntactically valid code that violates governor limits, uses deprecated components, or misunderstands the Salesforce execution model.

The Claude + Salesforce partnership changes this because it was designed specifically to address it.

Read: Agentforce and the Future of Enterprise AI

What Claudeforce Actually Means for Developers

When Salesforce and Anthropic announced Claudeforce on August 26, 2026, most coverage focused on the business side — sellers accessing Salesforce data inside Claude, AI agents resolving customer cases. These are real and significant. But the developer story is equally significant and received far less attention.

Two things happened that directly affect how Salesforce applications are built:

First: Salesforce formally made Claude Code and Claude Enterprise its preferred AI tool for all developers and knowledge workers across the organization. This is not a vendor preference — it is an official adoption decision, with Salesforce’s own engineering teams now using Claude Code as their development tool of choice.

Second: Salesforce shipped an official Salesforce Development Plugin for Claude Code — the first official plugin in the Claude Plugin Marketplace built specifically for a development platform. This plugin does not just add Salesforce syntax awareness to Claude. It packages Salesforce-specific skills, MCP servers, specialized development agents, hooks, and commands into a single installation that transforms Claude Code from a general-purpose coding assistant into a Salesforce development expert.

Jay Hurst, SVP of Product Management at Salesforce, demonstrated the capability at Dreamforce 2026. His summary of the developer experience: “When I’m ready, all I have to say is, ‘Claude, let’s build it.’”

Let us look at what that actually means across the specific development scenarios Salesforce engineers encounter every day.

Also read: How We Built a Duplicate Lead Detection Solution Inside Salesforce

How Claude Changes Apex Development

Apex is where the complexity of Salesforce development is most concentrated, and where the gap between a developer who understands the platform and one who does not is most costly.

A well-written Apex trigger handles bulk operations correctly (processing records in sets, not one at a time), stays within governor limits (CPU time, SOQL queries, DML statements, heap size), includes proper exception handling, has test coverage that actually tests the behavior (not just covers lines), and follows the trigger framework pattern the organization has standardized on.

A poorly-written Apex trigger works in a developer sandbox with five records, fails when a data migration loads five thousand records into production, and produces debugging nightmares because the error context was not captured.

Claude, equipped with the Salesforce Development Plugin, generates Apex code with Salesforce-specific constraints built into the output:

  • Trigger logic written using collections and maps rather than per-record SOQL inside loops
  • Governor limit-aware code structure that prevents the most common production failures
  • Test classes that cover multiple scenarios — the happy path, the empty set, the bulk operation, the exception case
  • Exception handling that captures and logs errors in the format the org’s monitoring expects

More useful still is what Claude does when you show it existing code. The Salesforce Claude Framework (an open-source community project built on top of the official plugin) adds automatic code-check hooks that detect hardcoded Salesforce IDs, hardcoded URLs, non-bulkified triggers, and other anti-patterns — flagging them before they are deployed rather than after they cause production incidents.

The practical effect is not that developers no longer need to understand Apex. It is that the Apex they write with Claude assistance starts from a correct foundation rather than requiring multiple review cycles to reach one.

How Claude Changes Lightning Web Component Development

Lightning Web Components have a steeper initial learning curve than most modern JavaScript frameworks. The reason is Salesforce-specific: LWC layers a declarative Salesforce data model on top of standard web component architecture, and the patterns for getting that right are not intuitive for developers coming from React, Vue, or Angular.

The most common LWC development mistakes are:

  • Using @wire adapters incorrectly (wrong properties, missing error handling, not accounting for loading state)
  • Building components that are not accessible (missing aria attributes, incorrect focus management)
  • Creating deeply nested component trees that produce unnecessary network calls
  • riting JavaScript that does not account for the LWC sandbox execution model

Claude with Salesforce-specific context generates LWC code that accounts for these patterns — using the correct syntax for wire adapters, building in error and loading state handling, and following the component design principles that make components reusable and maintainable. The Salesforce MCP Server for Claude Code includes a dedicated lwc-experts agent specifically optimized for component analysis, best practices, and optimization.

This matters for enterprise application development because LWC component quality directly affects both the end-user experience and the long-term maintainability of the application. Components built correctly the first time require significantly less rework during the lifetime of the application.

How Claude Changes SOQL and Data Layer Work

SOQL queries are not SQL. They have selectivity requirements, relationship traversal constraints, and limitations on what operations can be performed in what context. A SOQL query that retrieves records efficiently in a small dataset can produce query timeout errors in a production org with millions of records if the query is not selective enough.

Claude with Salesforce context can:

  • Review SOQL queries for selectivity issues (fields that are not indexed, filters that produce full table scans)
  • Identify relationship queries that traverse too many levels or generate implicit joins that are expensive at scale
  • Flag SOQL inside loops (the most common source of governor limit violations)
  • Suggest query restructuring that achieves the same result with better index utilization

For data-intensive Salesforce implementations — financial services, healthcare, manufacturing — this query review capability is immediately valuable. Production query timeouts are expensive to diagnose and fix; catching the problem at code review is significantly cheaper.

How Claude Changes Agentforce Development

The newest and potentially most significant way Claude is changing Salesforce development is in how Agentforce agents are built.

Agentforce Vibes is Salesforce’s development and testing environment for AI agents — and Claude is the default model in Vibes. This means the environment where developers build, test, and debug Agentforce agents is powered by the same Claude model that will power the agents in production. What you see in Vibes is what you ship.

The practical workflow change is significant. Building an Agentforce agent previously meant understanding Agent Builder’s UI, defining topics and actions manually, and testing through iterative configuration cycles. With Claude as the reasoning model in Vibes, developers can:

  • Describe the agent’s intended behavior in natural language and let Claude generate the initial topic and action configuration
  • Ask Claude to explain why an agent made a particular decision in a test scenario — the Vibes trace view shows Claude’s reasoning path, not just the input and output
  • Iterate on agent behavior through conversational follow-up: “make this agent escalate to a human if the account is flagged as at-risk,” “add a step that checks inventory before confirming the order”

For organizations deploying Agentforce at scale, this iterative, conversational development model compresses the time from agent concept to production-ready configuration — which Salesforce’s own data shows has reduced by 53% across its customer base in the past year.

Check: Talend + Salesforce Integration — How to Build Efficient, Scalable Data Pipelines

The MCP Architecture: Connecting Claude to Your Org

One of the most powerful but least-publicized capabilities in the Claude + Salesforce combination is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration that allows Claude Code to connect directly to your Salesforce org.

The Salesforce MCP Server for Claude Code provides 60+ tools covering:

  • Metadata management (retrieve, deploy, and manage Salesforce metadata)
  • Data operations (query, insert, update, delete against org data)
  • Testing tools (run unit tests, review test results)
  • LWC development support (component analysis, lint checks)
  • Deployment operations (validate and deploy changes to connected orgs)

This means Claude Code is not just writing Salesforce code in isolation. It is connected to the actual org — able to retrieve the existing metadata schema, understand what custom objects and fields already exist, run tests against real configurations, and deploy changes directly.

For developers, this shifts Claude from a code suggestion engine to an active development partner that works within the context of your actual Salesforce environment, not a generic representation of what Salesforce environments typically look like.

What This Means for Enterprise Development Teams

The combination of Claude Code, the Salesforce Development Plugin, the MCP server, and Agentforce Vibes changes several dimensions of how enterprise Salesforce development teams operate:

Faster onboarding for new developers. New Salesforce developers typically take three to six months before they are writing production-quality Apex and LWC independently. Claude’s Salesforce-specific knowledge — governor limits, anti-patterns, correct wire adapter usage — gives new developers a guardrail that catches the most common mistakes before they reach code review. Junior developers supported by Claude produce output that more consistently matches the quality standard senior developers would apply.

More consistent code quality at scale. In a large Salesforce development organization, code quality varies with the experience level of the individual developer. Automatic anti-pattern detection, governor limit checks, and LWC best practice enforcement in the development tool — rather than only in code review — raises the floor across the team.

Faster iteration on Agentforce deployments. As Agentforce moves from pilot to production across enterprise Salesforce customers, the speed at which agents can be built, tested, and refined becomes a competitive factor. Development teams using Claude in Agentforce Vibes iterate through agent configurations in conversations rather than through manual UI cycles.

Better documentation as a natural output. One of the least glamorous but most practically costly problems in Salesforce development is the documentation gap — code that works but has no documentation, configurations that exist but have no written explanation of why. Claude generates documentation alongside code as a natural part of the development process, reducing the technical debt that accumulates when documentation is treated as optional.

Getting Started: The Practical Steps

If you are a Salesforce developer or a leader of a Salesforce development team, here is how to engage with the Claude + Salesforce capability today:

Step 1 — Install Claude Code. Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-based AI development tool. You will need Claude Code version 2.1.222 or later. A Salesforce Foundations or Agentforce license provides direct access to the Salesforce Development Plugin.

Step 2 — Install the Salesforce Development Plugin. From a terminal, run: claude plugin install salesforce-development@claude-plugins-official. Start a Claude Code session and run /plugin to verify installation.

Step 3 — Configure the Salesforce MCP Server. Add the Salesforce DX MCP Server to your Claude Code configuration to connect Claude directly to your org. This requires Salesforce CLI to be installed and your org authenticated.

Step 4 — Connect a Salesforce DX project. Set up a Salesforce DX project in your development environment and connect it to your sandbox or developer org. The plugin’s workflows operate within the DX project structure.

Step 5 — Start with a specific use case. The most effective way to evaluate the capability is to apply it to real work — a specific Apex class you need to write, a specific LWC component you need to build, or a specific Agentforce agent you need to configure. Real-work application gives you a concrete basis for assessing the quality and speed improvement rather than an abstract evaluation.

Also check: External Services in Salesforce - Connect Any REST API Without Writing a Line of Apex

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Salesforce Development Plugin for Claude Code?

The Salesforce Development Plugin is Salesforce’s first official plugin for Claude Code — Anthropic’s AI-powered command-line development tool. It packages Salesforce-specific skills, MCP servers, specialized agents, hooks, and commands into a single installation that makes Claude Code aware of Salesforce’s development patterns, governor limits, anti-patterns, and best practices. It was announced as part of the Claudeforce partnership in August 2026 and is available through the official Claude Plugin Marketplace.

How does Claude understand Salesforce-specific constraints like governor limits?

The Salesforce Development Plugin includes Salesforce-specific context and skills that encode the platform’s constraints — governor limits, bulkification requirements, wire adapter patterns, deployment rules — into Claude’s working knowledge. The Salesforce MCP Server also connects Claude directly to the actual org, allowing it to work with real schema and configuration rather than generic Salesforce knowledge.

Can Claude Code deploy to Salesforce?

Yes. The Salesforce MCP Server that connects to Claude Code includes deployment tools — allowing Claude Code to validate and deploy changes to connected Salesforce orgs directly from the development session. This keeps the deployment workflow within the same context as the development work rather than requiring a separate deployment process.

Does this replace Salesforce developers?

No. Claude with Salesforce context makes Salesforce developers more productive and helps less experienced developers produce higher-quality code faster. It does not replace the judgment required to design a data model correctly, make architectural decisions that will hold up as the business grows, debug complex multi-system integration failures, or manage the stakeholder relationships that determine whether a Salesforce implementation actually gets adopted. The expertise requirement changes in its composition — more time on design, architecture, and review; less time on boilerplate code generation and documentation.

Closing Thought

The Salesforce + Claude partnership is often described in terms of what business users can now do — sellers accessing CRM data inside Claude, Agentforce agents resolving customer cases autonomously. These are the use cases that make press releases.

The developer story is less flashy but arguably more transformative over time. The way enterprise applications are designed, built, tested, documented, and deployed on the Salesforce platform is changing — not because the platform changed, but because the tool developers use while building on it now understands the platform at a depth that has not previously been possible with AI assistance.

Jay Hurst’s framing at Dreamforce — “When I’m ready, all I have to say is, ‘Claude, let’s build it’” — captures the direction accurately.

The distance between idea and deployed, tested, documented Salesforce application is getting shorter. That matters for the businesses that run on Salesforce and for the development teams that build for them.

medium.titulo: I Built an AI-Powered Bot to Automate My Bookkeeping
medium.resumo: A system that runs Claude Code on Google Cloud and uses it as an LLM endpoint to automate my bookkeeping.
medium.conteudo_html:
A system that runs Claude Code on Google Cloud and uses it as an LLM endpoint to automate my bookkeeping.

💡 Note 1: The most interesting part is how the AI is plugged in: I’m running the Claude Code CLI inside a Google Cloud Run container, using my existing Claude subscription. If that’s the part you came for, jump to “Part 1: The Backend” section.
⚠️ Note 2: This is not an industry-scale project. It’s a personal utility built for one user (me). The architecture is intentionally simple and not designed to scale. Take the ideas, not the SLA.

The Problem

I use Google Sheets to manage my finances because it's flexible and extensible. Unlike most budgeting apps, I can customize it to fit my exact needs instead of being limited by the features the app provides.

The problem was the data entry.

Every night, I had to sit at my laptop, remember what I had spent that day, dig through messages, and enter everything into the sheet.

So I kept asking myself one question: how do I reduce the effort of recording a transaction?

The Solution (Version 1)

The goal was simple: I send a quick text about a transaction from my phone, and a new row appears in my sheet.

Version 1 has two parts:

  1. The backend. A small Node.js service on Google Cloud Run that does all the work. It receives the message, uses AI to turn it into a transaction, writes the row to Google Sheets, and replies with a confirmation.
  2. The user interface. A Telegram chat with my own bot.

Part 1: The Backend

For every message, the backend does four things:

  1. Receives the text from Telegram via a Cloud Run endpoint.
  2. Asks AI to turn it into a structured transaction.
  3. Writes the transaction to the right row in my sheet.
  4. Replies in Telegram with what it added.

The second one is the interesting part.

Which AI, and where to plug it in?

The usual answer is to “Use AI”: get an API key, call the API, and pay per token. That works fine. But I was already paying for a Claude Code subscription, and Claude Code has a feature I use all the time locally:

claude -p "your prompt here"

-p (print mode) runs Claude non-interactively. You pass it a prompt, it prints the answer, and it exits, a bit like python -c "..." but for an AI.

So the idea was simple: if I can run claude -p inside my Cloud Run container, the backend can call Claude like any other command-line tool.

How it works

1. Install Claude Code in the container. It’s an npm package, so it goes in package.json like any other dependency:

"dependencies": {
  "@anthropic-ai/claude-code": "^2.1.140",
  "@google-cloud/firestore": "^7.10.0",
  "googleapis": "^144.0.0"
}

The claude binary lands in node_modules/.bin, and the Dockerfile adds that folder to PATH.

2. Authenticate with the subscription, not an API key. On my laptop, I ran:

claude setup-token

This creates a long-lived OAuth token tied to my Claude subscription. I pass it to Cloud Run as the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN environment variable, and the CLI uses it automatically. No browser login.

⚠️ This setup is fine for a single-user personal tool. If you’re building something for public, use a proper Anthropic API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) and check Anthropic's usage terms.

3. Call it from Node.js. The backend spawns the CLI as a child process:

const { stdout } = await execFile(
  "claude",
  ["-p", "--model", "sonnet", "--output-format", "json", prompt],
  { env: { ...process.env, HOME: "/tmp" } },
);

The flags I use:

4. Teach Claude my spreadsheet. The prompt does the heavy lifting. It tells Claude:

  • The exact JSON shape to return, and to return only JSON
  • How to decide type: money received ("salary", "got", "refund") is income; everything else is expense
  • Today’s date, so “yesterday” or “last Friday” resolves correctly
  • The exact category lists from my sheet, and it must pick one of them (falling back to Other)

What claude -p --output-format json returns for "Groceries 3000":

{
  "type": "result",
  "subtype": "success",
  "is_error": false,
  "duration_ms": 4210,
  "total_cost_usd": 0.011,
  "result": "{\"type\":\"expense\",\"date\":\"2026-06-07\",\"amount\":3000,\"currency\":\"LKR\",\"description\":\"Groceries\",\"category\":\"Food\"}"
}

The result field is the transaction. Claude is the translator between "how I talk" and "how my spreadsheet thinks".

Writing to the sheet

My Transactions tab has two tables:

  • Expenses: Date, Amount, Description, Category
  • Income: Date, Amount, Description, Category

Each has a fixed list of categories (Food, Transportation, Utilities, Home, … for expenses, and Paycheck, Bonus, Interest, Other for income).

A transaction is either an expense or an income, and the backend picks the table from type. It finds the last filled row in that table and writes the new row right after it with the Sheets API (values.batchUpdate), for example B42:E42 → 2026-06-07 | 3000 | Groceries | Food.

Note: To let Cloud Run access my private sheet, I used a Google service account. I attached it to the Cloud Run service and shared the sheet with its email as an Editor. No key files are needed. The service account only gives the backend access to the sheet.

Part 2: The User Interface (Telegram)

My phone is always with me, and so is Telegram, so a chat with a bot is the whole UI.

I created a bot with @BotFather (it takes two minutes and gives you a bot token) and registered a webhook. Telegram POSTs every message I send the bot to the backend, and the backend replies through the Bot API.

What Telegram sends the backend:

POST /telegram
X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: <my webhook secret>
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "update_id": 90817263,
  "message": {
    "message_id": 512,
    "chat": { "id": 123456789 },
    "date": 1780848000,
    "text": "lunch 850 food"
  }
}

Two cheap layers of protection:

  • Webhook secret. When you register a webhook, you can give Telegram a secret_token. Telegram sends it back in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header on every call. The backend rejects any request without it, so random people hitting the URL get a 401.
  • Chat allowlist. ALLOWED_CHAT_IDS holds my own Telegram chat ID. Even if someone finds my bot, they can't write to my sheet.

The Architecture So Far

This is the first version that actually worked. I typelunch 850, a row appears, and I get a confirmation. That alone removed most of the friction.

The Over-Engineering (Version 2)

Bank SMS as the trigger

Lazy me didn’t even want to send a Telegram message for every transaction 😃.

Almost all my transactions are digital. I rarely pay cash. Every card swipe and transfer already sends me an SMS from my bank. That SMS is the event. I just needed to catch it.

On the iPhone (Android also has apps for this), I used the Shortcuts app → Automation → Message. When a message arrives from my bank’s sender ID, an automation POSTs the raw SMS to a new endpoint on my API:

POST /ingest
X-Ingest-Secret: <a separate shared secret>
Content-Type: application/json
{ "text": "Auth Pmt of LKR 2,350.00 at KEELLS SUPER on 07/06/26 using card ending 1234" }

Then I gave Claude a second, separate prompt for reading Bank SMS.

Letting Claude ask me questions

New problem. When the SMS names a merchant, Sonnet is usually smart enough to work out the category and description on its own. But some messages are just:

LKR 5,493.00 debited from your A/c ****1234 via Outward CEFT on 12/06/2026

That’s money leaving my account, so it’s definitely an expense. But for what? Rent? A friend? Groceries? There’s no way to tell.

So I told Claude: don’t guess. If you can’t classify it confidently, return "type": "unclear". The driver then asks me on Telegram:

❓ Not sure how to classify this SMS:
LKR 5,493.00 debited from your A/c ****1234 via Outward CEFT on 12/06/2026

It’s two-way now. But there’s an async problem. I might answer in five minutes or in five hours. A Cloud Run request can’t sit there holding the original SMS while it waits for me, and it shouldn’t. The container should finish its work and scale down.

Making it async with Firestore

Another round of over-engineering 😃

  1. The bot sends the question to Telegram, and Telegram returns the message_id of that question.
  2. The driver saves the original SMS in Firestore, using that message_id as the document key. Then the request ends and the container is free to scale to zero.
  3. Hours later, I quote-reply the question in Telegram (swipe to reply) with something like expense rent home.
  4. Telegram includes reply_to_message.message_id in the update. The API sees it's a reply, looks up that ID in Firestore, and gets the original SMS back.
  5. Claude receives both the original SMS (for amount and date) and my answer (for type, category, and description), builds the transaction, and the row is written. The Firestore record is then deleted.

Keying on the question message_id has a nice side effect: several questions can be open at once without getting mixed up. A normal (non-quoted) message is always a brand-new transaction, so an old unanswered question can never hijack it. Replying ignore to a question simply dismisses it.

Guardrails: OTPs, promotions, and other noise

Banks don’t only send transaction alerts. They also send OTPs, promotions, balance alerts, fixed-deposit renewals, and “payment received” notices when I pay off my own credit card. None of those belong in my budget.

There are two layers of defence:

  1. On the phone. The Shortcut automation doesn’t fire for obvious noise like OTP messages, so they never leave the device.
  2. In Claude. The SMS prompt has a fourth type, "ignore", with an explicit list of what counts as a non-transaction. When Claude ignores something, the bot still tells me:

⏭️ Skipped (Fixed deposit renewal, not a transaction): Your FD ****5678 has been renewed for 3 Month(s)…

Every skip notification shows me something the phone automation let through, which helps me tighten the Shortcut filter over time.

Each bank SMS ends up in one of three outcomes

The Final Architecture

Conclusion

My bookkeeping went from a nightly chore to something I barely notice. Most transactions log themselves from bank SMS. The odd cash payment is a three-word Telegram message. The rare ambiguous one is a quick quote-reply whenever I get to it.

The bigger takeaway: Claude Code isn’t just a coding assistant in your terminal. With -p, it's a general-purpose reasoning step you can drop into any backend, using the subscription you already have.

Nothing here is specific to money, either. Strip away the finance parts, and you get a reusable pattern:

Logging receipts, tracking workouts, sorting school notices, building a reading list, keeping a home-maintenance log: if it’s personal, repetitive, and text-shaped, the same pattern fits. You don’t need an industry-scale platform. A small Cloud Run service, an AI subscription you already pay for, and an evening of vibe-coding with Claude can take one more chore off your plate.

Happy automating!

medium.titulo: I built a Vue directive that turns your real component into its own skeleton
medium.resumo: Skeleton loaders have a maintenance problem. You build a second version of every component by hand: a grey circle where the avatar goes…
medium.conteudo_html:
Skeleton loaders have a maintenance problem. You build a second version of every component by hand: a grey circle where the avatar goes, three bars where the text goes. Then someone adds a badge to the real card, and the skeleton quietly stops matching.

I wanted the skeleton to come from the component itself. So I built v-skeleton, a directive in vue-smart-loading-kit:

While loading is true, every line of text becomes a bar, images and buttons become solid blocks, and borders and spacing stay exactly as they are. When loading ends, the real content is back. Try it in the live demo (Skeletonize page, tick "loading").

This post is about how it works, and about the bugs that only showed up because of how I tested it.

The rule: never change the DOM

The obvious approach is to measure the real elements and render placeholder boxes over them. That needs JavaScript on every render, and every resize, and it fights with your layout.

I took the opposite route. The directive only toggles a class, a few CSS variables and two attributes on the element:

Everything else is CSS. No element is added, removed or resized, so nothing can move. That turned out to be the most important design decision, and the hardest to keep.

Hiding text without breaking borders

My first version hid text with color: transparent. It looked right until a code review found that it also erased every border, divider and icon that uses currentColor. A card with a 1px solid currentColor border lost its border.

The fix is a property most people never touch:

text-fill-color paints only the glyphs. color, and everything that inherits it through currentColor, keeps its real value.

One bar per line of text

To draw bars where the lines are, I mask the element’s background with a repeating gradient sized by the lh unit (one line-height):

Each line gets a bar, with a gap between lines. A paragraph that wraps to three lines gets three bars, at whatever width the browser chose.

Masking the whole element has a side effect: it also hides the element’s own border, which matters for table cells. So the mask has two more layers, a border-box layer and a padding-box layer combined with mask-composite: exclude. Together they leave a ring where the border is, so table grid lines survive.

Images get object-position: -99999px, which slides the picture out of its own box while the box keeps its size and radius. Buttons and inputs become solid blocks.

Proving that nothing moves

“Nothing moves” is easy to claim and hard to test. jsdom, which most Vue tests run in, has no layout engine: every element is 0×0, so any position assertion passes.

So the visual rules are tested in a real Chromium with Vitest Browser Mode and Playwright. The main test records the bounding box of every element, turns the skeleton on, and records them again:

It runs in CI on every push, so any CSS change that shifts a single pixel fails the build.

The SSR bug I almost shipped

With server rendering and placeholder data, you want the skeleton in the server HTML, so fake content never flashes. Directives don’t run on the server, but Vue has a getSSRProps hook for exactly this, and Vue 3.5's data-allow-mismatch lets hydration accept the attributes the client sets again.

The bug was in restoring attributes. When the skeleton ends, the directive puts back whatever inert and aria-hidden the element had before. My first version read "before" from the DOM. After SSR, the DOM already contained the skeleton's own inert, so it saved inert as the original value. When loading ended, it restored it, and the whole section stayed unclickable forever.

The fix was to read the original values from the vnode, which is what the template actually binds, never from the DOM. A test now server-renders, hydrates, ends the load and checks that no attribute is left behind.

Timing: when to show it at all

A skeleton that flashes for 80ms on a fast request feels worse than no skeleton. So v-skeleton waits 200ms before showing anything, and once shown it stays for at least 500ms so it never blinks off:

The timing tests use fake timers and record the value at every 10ms step, so a single wrong frame fails them. Checking only the final state would miss a flash in the middle.

What 100% coverage missed

The package had about 99% line coverage, and I still didn’t know whether the tests would notice a broken default. So I ran Stryker, which plants small bugs in the source (flips a condition, changes a constant, drops a call) and reruns the tests for each one.

The first score was 80%. Some of the surviving mutants were real gaps: you could change the table skeleton’s default row height and no test failed. Two were real bugs:

  • v-skeleton removed an aria-hidden that the template had bound to false, while Vue itself renders it as "false".
  • The color helper accepted #12345z as a valid hex color, because parseInt("5z", 16) stops at the bad digit and returns 5.

After closing the gaps the score is above 90%. The rest are mostly equivalent mutants, changes no test could observe, which is why 100% isn’t the goal.

Limits

It’s CSS, so it has CSS’s blind spots. The last line of a wrapped paragraph gets a full-width bar, because CSS can’t know where the text ends. A few characters on a colored circle (an initials avatar) look like text, so you mark them data-skeleton="block". And it needs browsers from late 2023 on, for :has(), lh and mask-composite.

Try it

npm install vue-smart-loading-kit

The kit also has a SmartLoader component with an error state and retry, 13 skeleton variants, 9 spinners and progress bars.

I’d love feedback, especially on layouts where the skeleton doesn’t look right.

medium.resumo: SaaS Laravel: Stop Rebuilding the Same SaaS Features Every Time. Starting a new SaaS product is exciting.
medium.conteudo_html:
SaaS Laravel: Stop Rebuilding the Same SaaS Features Every Time. Starting a new SaaS product is exciting.

You have an idea, you know what you want to build, and you want to start working on the part that actually makes your product different.

Then reality hits.

Before you can work on the real product, you end up building the same things again:

  • Authentication
  • User profiles
  • Teams
  • Permissions
  • Invitations
  • Notifications
  • Settings
  • Activity logs
  • Dashboard layouts
  • Account management
  • Frontend components
  • Error states
  • Email flows

None of these features are unusual.

But almost every SaaS application needs them.

And rebuilding them for every new project takes a lot of time.

That is why I built SaaS Laravel.

Website: https://saas-laravel.com/

What Is SaaS Laravel?

SaaS Laravel is a set of Laravel starter kits built for developers who want a solid starting point for a SaaS application.

The idea is simple:

Start with the common SaaS work already organized, then spend your time building your actual product.

It is not a no-code platform.

It is not a closed system.

And it is not trying to hide Laravel from you.

You still work with your Laravel application normally. You own the code, you can change it, extend it, remove parts you do not need, or build completely new features on top of it.

SaaS Laravel simply gives you a better place to start.

Why I Built It

Whenever I started a new SaaS project, I noticed the same pattern.

I would spend the first few days or weeks rebuilding things I had already built before.

Create authentication.

Create the dashboard.

Add user settings.

Add team members.

Create invitations.

Add permissions.

Create notifications.

Build common frontend components.

Handle empty states.

Add profile pages.

Set up project structure.

And only after all of that could I start working on the feature that actually made the product interesting.

That felt wasteful.

So instead of rebuilding the same foundation for every project, I wanted one clean base that I could reuse.

That became SaaS Laravel.

Start With the Essentials Already in Place

A starter kit should save time without making the code difficult to understand.

That is why SaaS Laravel focuses on features that most SaaS products need sooner or later.

You start with a working foundation and then shape it around your product.

Some of the common pieces include:

  • Authentication
  • User accounts
  • Teams
  • Member management
  • Permissions
  • Invitations
  • Notifications
  • Settings
  • Activity-related features
  • Reusable UI
  • Common layouts
  • Developer-friendly project structure

Instead of starting from an empty project, you start from something that already feels like an application.

Authentication Is Already Part of the Foundation

Authentication is usually one of the first things we build.

Login.

Registration.

Password reset.

Email verification.

Account-related pages.

It is necessary, but it is rarely the reason someone is building a SaaS product.

SaaS Laravel gives you a working authenticated application so you can move on to more important product work.

You can still customize the flow whenever your application needs something different.

Teams Without Building Everything From Scratch

A lot of SaaS products eventually become multi-user products.

One person creates an account.

Then they want to invite a teammate.

Then another.

Soon you need:

  • Team members
  • Invitations
  • Access control
  • Member management
  • Different permissions

This can quickly become a project of its own.

SaaS Laravel gives this part a clear structure from the beginning.

Instead of figuring out the entire team system while building your actual product, you already have a foundation you can extend.

Simple Permission Management

Not every user should be able to do everything.

An owner may have full access.

Another user may only be able to view data.

Someone else may be able to create records but not delete them.

These rules become important very quickly in real SaaS products.

SaaS Laravel includes a straightforward permission approach so your application can control access without turning permission management into unnecessary complexity.

The important part is that you can adapt it to your own product rules.

Invitations That Feel Like Part of the Product

Inviting someone sounds like a small feature.

But once you build it properly, you need to think about:

  • Who can invite users?
  • What happens if the email is already registered?
  • What happens if it is not?
  • When does an invitation expire?
  • Can it be resent?
  • Can it be cancelled?
  • What access should the invited person receive?

These are small decisions individually, but together they take time.

A starter kit should give you a sensible starting point instead of making you solve the same problem again.

Notifications Without Reinventing the UI

Notifications appear in almost every modern application.

A team member joins.

Something is updated.

A task completes.

An invitation arrives.

An important action needs the user’s attention.

Creating the backend event is only one part of the job.

You also need a usable interface for displaying notifications and handling read/unread states.

SaaS Laravel provides a foundation for this so notifications can feel like a normal part of your application instead of another standalone feature you need to design from zero.

Settings Should Be Easy to Extend

Every application eventually grows a settings area.

At first, maybe it is only the user’s name and email.

Later you may need:

  • Account settings
  • Team settings
  • Application preferences
  • Notification preferences
  • Security settings
  • Product-specific configuration

SaaS Laravel gives settings a clear home in the application.

You can keep adding your own options without turning the settings area into an unorganized collection of pages.

A UI You Can Actually Change

A starter kit should not force you to keep its design forever.

Your product will have its own brand.

Its own colors.

Its own layout decisions.

Its own components.

That is expected.

The purpose of the included UI is to save you from beginning with a blank page.

Use it as it is when it works for you.

Change it when it does not.

The code is yours.

Choose Your Frontend

Different developers prefer different frontend frameworks.

Some prefer Vue.

Some work faster in React.

Others enjoy Svelte.

SaaS Laravel is designed around that reality.

You can choose the frontend you are comfortable with instead of changing your entire development workflow just because a starter kit picked one framework.

The available starter-kit options include:

  • Vue
  • React
  • Svelte

The important part is that they share the same Laravel foundation.

One Laravel Foundation, Multiple Frontend Choices

Maintaining separate Laravel applications for Vue, React, and Svelte would create unnecessary duplication.

Fix something in one project and you would have to repeat the same change in the others.

That is exactly what I wanted to avoid.

The goal of SaaS Laravel is to keep the common backend foundation consistent while allowing different frontend implementations.

Conceptually:

Laravel
                │
        Shared SaaS Core
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      │         │         │
     Vue      React     Svelte

The business foundation stays familiar.

You choose how you want to render the product.

Use It As-Is or Make It Yours

SaaS Laravel is not intended to be a rigid template.

Think of it as a starting point.

Maybe you need everything it provides.

Maybe you only need half of it.

That is fine.

You can:

  • Remove features
  • Rename things
  • Change layouts
  • Replace components
  • Add your own modules
  • Change the data model
  • Build your own business logic
  • Customize the frontend completely

A starter kit should make your first steps faster, not decide what your final product must look like.

Built for Real Development

A polished screenshot is nice.

But developers eventually have to work with the code.

That is why project structure matters.

When a project grows, you need to know where things belong.

You should be able to open the application a few months later and still understand how it is organized.

SaaS Laravel aims to keep the structure predictable so adding new features does not slowly turn the project into something difficult to maintain.

Common Components Save More Time Than You Think

Buttons, inputs, selects, checkboxes, labels and validation messages seem small.

But when every page creates its own version, inconsistency starts to appear quickly.

One button looks different.

Another input handles errors differently.

One page uses a different spacing system.

A reusable component layer helps keep those small details consistent.

That means when you improve one common component, many parts of the application improve with it.

Built With Customization in Mind

There is a big difference between a starter kit and a finished SaaS product.

Your product will still need its own:

  • Database design
  • Business rules
  • Workflows
  • Features
  • Branding
  • Integrations
  • Emails
  • Pricing
  • Product experience

And that is exactly where your development time should go.

The starter kit handles the common foundation.

You build the part people are actually paying for.

Developer Experience Matters

A good starter kit should reduce friction.

You should not spend hours trying to understand why something was built in an unusual way.

The code should feel familiar to someone already comfortable with Laravel.

That is also why I prefer keeping the product close to normal Laravel development rather than hiding everything behind proprietary abstractions.

You are still building a Laravel application.

You simply begin further ahead.

AI Coding Tools Work Better With Consistent Structure

AI coding assistants are becoming part of normal development workflows.

But they work much better when a project has clear patterns.

If one feature uses one folder structure and the next feature uses a completely different approach, generated code can quickly become inconsistent.

A predictable starter-kit structure gives both developers and coding agents a clearer pattern to follow.

For example, instead of asking an AI agent to invent an entire user-management architecture, you can ask it to extend the existing structure.

That usually produces cleaner results and requires less cleanup afterwards.

You Still Own the Code

This is important.

SaaS Laravel is meant to help developers build their own products.

It should not turn your application into something you cannot control.

You get the code.

You work with it directly.

You can understand it.

And you can change it.

There is no reason your SaaS product should become dependent on a visual builder or proprietary runtime just because you wanted to save some development time at the beginning.

Who Is SaaS Laravel For?

SaaS Laravel can be useful if you are:

  • Building your first SaaS
  • Launching another SaaS product
  • Creating an internal business tool
  • Building a client SaaS application
  • Prototyping a product
  • Creating a micro-SaaS
  • Working alone
  • Working with a small team

It is especially useful if you already know Laravel and want to spend less time rebuilding common application infrastructure.

Who Probably Does Not Need It?

Not every project needs a starter kit.

If you are building a very small application with only one or two pages, starting with a fresh Laravel installation may be perfectly fine.

And if your project has an extremely unusual architecture, you may prefer building everything yourself.

SaaS Laravel is most useful when your project looks like a typical modern SaaS application and you would otherwise spend time recreating the same common features.

The Goal Is Simple: Ship Faster

The goal is not to generate an entire SaaS business for you.

The goal is to remove unnecessary repetition.

Instead of this:

New idea
   ↓
Build authentication
   ↓
Build dashboard
   ↓
Build teams
   ↓
Build permissions
   ↓
Build invitations
   ↓
Build notifications
   ↓
Build settings
   ↓
Finally start the product

You can get closer to this:

New idea
   ↓
Start with SaaS Laravel
   ↓
Customize the foundation
   ↓
Build your actual product

That is the difference I wanted from a starter kit.

One-Time Access

I also wanted the purchasing model to stay simple.

Instead of another recurring development subscription, the starter kits are offered with one-time access.

Choose the framework you actually use, or get access to the complete set if you work across multiple frontend stacks.

The current options and details are available directly on the website.

View the starter kits:
https://saas-laravel.com/

Start With a Better Foundation

Building a SaaS product is already difficult.

There are plenty of real problems to solve:

Finding customers.

Building something useful.

Improving onboarding.

Listening to feedback.

Fixing bugs.

Shipping new features.

You probably do not need to add “build another settings screen from scratch” to that list.

That is what SaaS Laravel is for.

A clean starting point.

Common SaaS features already organized.

Laravel code you can actually work with.

And the freedom to turn it into your own product.

If you are starting a Laravel SaaS and want to spend more time on the product instead of rebuilding the foundation, take a look:

SaaS Laravel
https://saas-laravel.com/

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Nike enfrenta crise com ações em baixa e anuncia demissões. Cuidado com o boato do "tênis que troca marcha" da Adidas: é apenas um protótipo. Inscrições para a Maratona de Maringá e corrida do Iron Maiden estão esgotadas. Infelizmente, um corredor morre atropelado em Roraima.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Segunda-feira | 5 de outubro de 2026

A situação da Nike está cada vez pior. Além da queda contínua das ações, que atingiram o menor patamar em 13 anos, a empresa agora anunciou um plano de demissões. Segundo a Forbes, as ações recuaram 3,8%, para US$ 33,80, o valor mais baixo desde setembro de 2013. A receita do primeiro trimestre ficou em US$ 11,2 bilhões, abaixo da estimativa de US$ 11,3 bilhões, uma queda atribuída principalmente à retração nas vendas na China, Europa, Oriente Médio e África. Para reverter o quadro, a empresa anunciou o “Nike Pace”, um novo modelo operacional que visa reduzir custos, modernizar a cadeia de suprimentos e reorganizar a liderança. Esse plano resultará em menos cargos, com as demissões começando em 2027. Desde o pico em 2021, quando as ações valiam US$ 179, a queda já chega a 76%. Nesse período, a Nike perdeu espaço para concorrentes como Hoka, On Running, Adidas e Puma, além de enfrentar o avanço de marcas esportivas chinesas como Anta e Li-Ning em seu próprio mercado.

O “tênis que troca marcha” da Adidas

Um vídeo viralizou nas redes sociais mostrando um suposto lançamento da Adidas: um tênis que “muda de marcha”. Cuidado para não cair nesse papo. Na verdade, trata-se de um protótipo, o Adizero Gearshift, apresentado no Adidas Lab, o laboratório de inovações da marca. O conceito permite ajustar a rigidez da placa de carbono com uma pequena alavanca. No entanto, isso é apenas um projeto experimental e não há qualquer previsão de que se torne um produto comercial. Muitas tecnologias testadas nos laboratórios das marcas nunca chegam ao público, então é preciso ter calma com essas novidades.

Última etapa do ASICS Run Challenge em Florianópolis

A última das seis etapas do circuito ASICS Run Challenge de 2026 acontecerá em Florianópolis no dia 8 de novembro. A prova, que oferece percursos de 4 km, 7 km e 15 km, é uma ótima oportunidade para quem busca se preparar para distâncias maiores. Se você quiser participar, pode usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para garantir 10% de desconto na sua inscrição.

Inscrições esgotadas em Maringá e na corrida do Iron Maiden

A primeira edição da Maratona Internacional de Maringá já é um sucesso. As inscrições para a prova de 42 km estão esgotadas. O evento, organizado pela Vô Esportes, terá transmissão ao vivo do Corrida no Ar. Outra prova que também esgotou rapidamente foi a “Run for Your Lives”, corrida oficial da banda Iron Maiden. Mesmo após a liberação de 1.000 vagas extras, todas as inscrições foram preenchidas.

Luto: corredor morre atropelado em Roraima

Infelizmente, temos mais uma notícia trágica no mundo da corrida. O corredor Giovanni Gameiro Gonzaga da Silva, de 43 anos, faleceu no último sábado em Roraima. Ele estava internado em estado grave desde sexta-feira, após ser atropelado enquanto fazia seu aquecimento. O motorista, que estava bêbado, foi encontrado dormindo dentro do carro após o acidente e teve sua prisão preventiva decretada. Nossos mais sinceros sentimentos à família e aos amigos de Giovanni.
